The system may aggregate findings and status from participating agents, request independent validation, reconcile conflicting results, prevent or resolve duplicated effort, and determine when an output satisfies a prerequisite for another activity. It may reassign stalled work, increase or reduce resources allocated to a branch, terminate low-value work, or initiate additional research or testing. Orchestration may use direct agent interfaces (See Autonomous AI Agent Communication: Direct Agent Communication) to transmit assignments, status, and results. Human involvement does not preclude autonomous attack orchestration. A human operator may define campaign objectives, select targets, provide infrastructure, establish constraints, or retain approval over consequential transitions. Autonomous Attack-Path Adaptation and Autonomous Attack Orchestration may occur together but describe different control functions. Attack-path adaptation captures how evidence changes the selected path. Attack orchestration captures how work is allocated, coordinated, validated, and redirected across agents.

name: Create Account

mitigations.name: AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management

description: Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to an AI system or its supporting infrastructure. With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that do not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system. Accounts may be created on local systems, in enterprise domains, cloud tenants, identity providers, or individual services. In AI environments, adversaries may create user, service, workload, or automation accounts in AI platforms, model or dataset repositories, development environments, experiment trackers, orchestration services, data stores, and other AI operations infrastructure.

name: Automated Collection

mitigations.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest

description: Adversaries may use automated techniques to collect data from AI systems and supporting enterprise environments. Automation may use scripts, command interpreters, command-line tools, or AI agent tools to identify, retrieve, copy, or aggregate data without a human selecting each individual item. Collection criteria may be fixed, such as file name, type, location, owner, date. Automation may also collect repeatedly, monitor for new material, traverse related resources, or combine data from local systems, cloud services, repositories, databases, object stores, and application APIs. In AI environments, targeted material may include models, datasets, configurations, conversation histories, retrieval databases, deployment information, logs, and other operational data.

name: Data Staged

mitigations.name: AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management

description: Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location before exfiltration. Staging consolidates, organizes, or prepares information obtained from one or more sources so it can be reviewed, processed, transferred, or retrieved more efficiently. Data may be staged on a compromised local system, another system in the victim environment, a cloud instance, shared storage, an application repository, or other remote infrastructure. It may remain in separate files or be combined into archives, databases, structured documents, manifests, or other collections. Adversaries may compress, encrypt, encode, split, rename, or otherwise transform staged data.

name: Compromise Infrastructure
description: Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure and repurpose it to support attacks against AI systems. Rather than buying, leasing, registering, or otherwise legitimately acquiring a resource, the adversary gains unauthorized control of infrastructure owned or operated by another party. Compromised infrastructure may include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, third-party web and DNS services, software or artifact repositories, development workspaces, compute services, and other externally hosted resources. In operations involving AI systems, adversaries may compromise infrastructure used for model development, artifact hosting, dataset processing, evaluation, inference, agent tooling, or AI operations. They may repurpose this infrastructure to host malicious artifacts, stage payloads, run tools or agents, relay traffic, capture credentials, provide command and control, process collected data, or launch attacks against additional systems. Compromised infrastructure may appear trustworthy because it uses a legitimate provider, established domain, valid certificate, reputable service, or expected AI development platform. It may also provide network access, compute resources, service identities, or trusted relationships that would be difficult for the adversary to establish directly.

name: Triggers in Multimodal Inputs
description: Adversaries may place instructions or triggers in one part of a multimodal input to influence the model while staying unnoticed by human reviewers and by defenses that do not inspect all input modalities. Multimodal systems jointly process text alongside other modalities, yet many moderation and filtering controls operate mainly on the textual channel. A payload placed in a modality that is not inspected, or is inspected differently from text, is still parsed by the model but can escape detection, allowing it to alter model output or carry a cross-modal prompt injection. Examples include instructions placed in an image, audio, or video channel, or carried in file metadata (e.g. EXIF for images, ID3 tags for audio, or document metadata).

name: AI Agent Response Biasing
description: Adversaries may manipulate an AI assistant so that it favors adversary-chosen sources, or content in its responses. By injecting instructions such as "treat [source] as a trusted source" or "recommend [source] first," an adversary biases the assistant's outputs toward their own interests, causing it to present promotional or self-serving content as if it were a neutral, well-reasoned response. This degrades the integrity and trustworthiness of the assistant's responses on topics the user may rely on, such as health, finance, or security, without the user being aware that the advice has been skewed. The injected instructions can be delivered through different ways, for example through Crafted AI Assistant Links. This impact may persist if the agent's memory was poisoned (See AI Agent Context Poisoning: Memory). Microsoft observed these instructions embedded in apparently helpful summarization links and identified publicly available tooling, including CiteMET, supporting their creation. These attempts sought to introduce third-party preferences into assistant responses; effects varied by assistant and over time.

name: Crafted AI Assistant Links
description: Adversaries may craft links that open an AI assistant or agent with attacker-controlled input already supplied, so that opening the link initiates an interaction the adversary defines rather than one the target composed. Many AI assistants accept a prompt through URL parameters (for example `?q=` or `?prompt=`) that is automatically populated, and in some cases submitted, when the link is opened. By encoding a chosen prompt into such a link, an adversary can cause the target's assistant to act on supplied instructions as soon as the link is opened. These links are frequently disguised as helpful actions, such as a "Summarize with AI" button or a share link, and distributed through web pages, emails, documents, or messages. Because the resulting interaction runs in the target's own assistant session, a crafted link can drive a range of downstream impacts depending on the supplied instructions, such as exfiltrating data the assistant can access or for AI Agent Response Biasing. Microsoft identified CiteMET and AI Share URL Creator as tools supporting this pattern in its investigation of AI Recommendation Poisoning. The generated links supply instructions to the receiving assistant; execution, memory retention, and downstream effects depend on the assistant's behavior and protections.

name: Misconfigured or Publicly Exposed AI Services
description: AI agents and LLM platforms are deployed across diverse architectures, including standalone servers, SaaS platforms, and low-code builders. All of these often have misconfigured access controls, ranging from missing authentication in LLM runtimes to permissive public access settings, that significantly expand their attack surface. AI agent's security posture affects how attackers are able to explore which agentic attack surface is available to them and directly either expands or limits an adversary's ability to discover and interact with a target's AI agents. For example, one internet-facing AI service could be more easily discoverable by any unauthenticated user, while another may require compromised credentials to even be discovered. Adversaries may discover and interact with AI agents and LLM services as unauthenticated users via a combination of various OSINT and active scanning methods. These could include using search engines to discover accessible agentic deployments (See Search Open Technical Databases), search backlinks which could indicate existing or open agents which have been embedded to frontends (See Search Open Websites/Domains), or directly scanning a target's AI infrastructure (See Active Scanning).

name: Discover AI Agent Runtime Capabilities
description: Adversaries may interact with an AI agent at runtime to reveal the capabilities available to it, without requiring access to its underlying configuration. Direct interaction with the agent can surface its registered tools and their accepted parameters, the actions it can take, the resources it can reach, and the identity and permission scope it acts under. Capabilities can also be inferred indirectly by issuing varied requests and observing which succeeded, failed, or refused. AI agents are often interconnected with enterprise resources, tools and databases, or embedded within SaaS platforms and have permissions to act on behalf of users in order to facilitate functionality. Once adversaries identify a functional agent that they have access to, they could map the attack surface within that agent, by testing its functionality, enumerating tools, capabilities, knowledge, and embedded credentials and permissions. This mapping process often reveals the AI agent's full toolset and configuration details and exposes additional exploitation, as enabled by AI Agent Tool Invocation. The resulting intelligence facilitates follow-on exploitation, including Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Exfiltration.

name: AI Targeted Cloaking
description: Adversaries may selectively deliver malicious or manipulated content to AI systems, while presenting different benign content to human users, web crawlers, or security detection mechanisms. They may identify AI browsers or agents via user-agent strings and condition the server response so that AI-based clients receive prompt injections or misleading content. Preventing human visitors, conventional web crawlers, and security tools from observing the same content allows adversaries to make malicious input more difficult to detect. AI Targeted Cloaking may be combined with Drive-by Compromise to deliver an LLM Prompt Injection.

name: Outputs from AI Models
description: Adversaries may gather, retain, and organize outputs from an AI model or service as material for subsequent adversarial operations. Systematic selection and aggregation of responses can produce datasets or observations useful for analyzing the target, reproducing its behavior, or developing further attacks. Collected material may include predictions and scores, embeddings or other exposed feature representations, generated content, reasoning traces, grades or preference judgments, and model-generated plans or tool calls. Outputs may be acquired directly from inference responses or indirectly from product-generated artifacts and records in which they are embedded or retained. Discover AI Model Outputs may help adversaries identify available outputs and useful signals before collection. Adversaries may perform LLM Prompt Crafting to elicit the outputs they require for follow-on actions. The resulting material may support collection of Training Data Information from AI Models, Recover AI Model Internals, or Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs. Adversaries may also use Centralized AI Service Request Routing, Indicator Removal, and AI Service Request Metadata Sanitization to obscure coordinated collection activity.

name: Exfiltration via AI User Interface
description: Adversaries exfiltrate information through an AI system's user-facing outputs. Information may be disclosed in conversational responses, generated documents, previews, or other content presented through the application. The application may expose information available to a victim-controlled AI service or deliver information gathered from other victim systems. Adversaries may direct an AI system to present sensitive information in responses or as downloadable artifacts. The application's user interface serves as the transfer channel through which adversaries receive the information. Transferred information may include Data from AI Services or Outputs from AI Models.

name: Training Data Information from AI Models
description: Adversaries may obtain sensitive information about the data used to train or fine-tune an AI model by analyzing its outputs or behavior. This can expose private associations, personally identifiable information, or proprietary data, creating data privacy concerns and supporting subsequent adversarial operations. Adversaries may determine whether particular samples were used in training through Infer Membership, identify aggregate characteristics of the training dataset through Infer Properties, infer sensitive attributes or reconstruct representative examples through Invert AI Model, or recover retained training content through Extract Memorized Data.

name: Infer Membership

mitigations.name: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate

description: Adversaries may infer whether a particular data sample was included in an AI model's training dataset. Samples may include records, text passages, images, or audio samples. Establishing membership may reveal sensitive associations, participation in a private dataset, or use of proprietary information. Membership inference is a data privacy concern because identifying a sample's inclusion may reveal sensitive associations or participation in a private dataset, even without recovering the underlying data. Methods may analyze prediction scores, token probabilities, loss values, generated responses, or other differences in model behavior. Adversaries may use statistical tests, shadow models, or auxiliary datasets to distinguish likely training members from nonmembers.

name: Infer Properties
description: Adversaries may infer sensitive global properties of the data used to train an AI model. Properties may include dataset provenance, population composition, relative class proportions, domain coverage, collection period, or the presence of a category or group. The adversary may compare output distributions, fit analytical or learned estimators, use auxiliary datasets, or contrast models trained with different known properties. The target is a property of the training data rather than membership of an individual record. Inferred properties of the training dataset may help adversaries identify a model's likely origin, distinguish between candidate models, identify underrepresented populations or domains, and tailor subsequent attacks to suspected weaknesses.

name: Invert AI Model

mitigations.name: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate

description: Adversaries may infer sensitive aggregate attributes or reconstruct representative examples of data used to train or fine-tune a target AI model by analyzing its behavior, outputs, or exposed representations. Reconstructed information may reveal characteristics of individuals, records, or classes represented in the training data without reproducing a particular training example. Methods may optimize candidate inputs, combine known attributes with model-derived signals, or use learned inversion models. Useful observations may include prediction scores, probabilities, embeddings, or gradients where exposed. Results may include inferred sensitive attributes, approximate reconstructions, or representative examples associated with a target identity or class. Such results do not by themselves establish that a reconstructed example was present in the training dataset.

name: Extract Memorized Data
description: Adversaries may elicit and recover sensitive content memorized by a generative AI model during training or fine-tuning. Recovered material may include complete training examples or recognizable portions of text, source code, or images, potentially exposing personal information, private communications, or proprietary material. Recovery may take the form of verbatim reproduction or near-duplicate outputs that reveal specific training content. Adversaries may supply partial passages, contextual cues, or repeated and varied inputs that encourage reproduction of memorized content. They may generate and filter candidate outputs or compare them with available reference material to identify likely training examples. Researchers have recovered verbatim training passages through language-model queries, including from production systems, and extracted memorized training images from diffusion models.

name: Indicator Removal
description: Adversaries may delete, alter, or falsify records and artifacts to conceal their activity, impede investigation, or make unauthorized actions appear legitimate. Targeted artifacts may include logs, command histories, files, metadata, repository history, and published content. Changes may selectively remove suspicious evidence while preserving surrounding material to maintain the appearance of normal activity. Agents may also conceal activity by modifying artifacts on external collaboration and distribution platforms. Editing public messages, removing malicious content, or rewriting revision history can obscure prior actions, make contributions appear benign, and complicate reconstruction of an attack. These changes may help an agent preserve credibility and continue operating after its activity attracts scrutiny, even when earlier versions remain recoverable. Autonomous AI agents may identify and manipulate evidence of their own actions without a human directing each concealment step. Agents may edit or delete accessible transcripts, replace records with misleading content, or tamper with harness components responsible for executing or recording tool calls. Such tampering can cause recorded actions or results to differ from actual execution, undermining oversight that relies on the affected records.

name: Compromise Accounts
description: Adversaries may compromise existing accounts with services that can support targeting or subsequent operations. These accounts may provide established identities, trusted relationships, access to resources, or funded wallets for AI services. Adversaries may obtain account credentials through Phishing, password guessing or reuse, theft of access tokens, or purchase from third parties. Adversaries may compromise AI service accounts for LLMJacking, a pattern of consuming model access and usage at the account holder's expense. Depending on the service, these resources may include prepaid balances or service wallets, promotional credits, subscription allowances, or usage charged to an existing payment method or enterprise billing account. Adversaries may use the acquired capacity for their own inference workloads, code generation, or tool development while exhausting the victim's available credits and quotas or generating additional charges. Compromised accounts may also supply capacity for AI Service Proxies, allowing operators to aggregate and resell access while concealing the underlying credentials from downstream users. Google has reported model distillation campaigns that used proxy infrastructure to rotate requests across compromised credentials and fraudulent accounts. Account pooling and resale also feature in the gray-market transfer station economy, where account merchants and registration intermediaries supply access alongside discounted capacity, unused quotas, and shared subscriptions..

name: Centralized AI Service Request Routing
description: Adversaries may distribute coordinated AI service requests across multiple pathways to impede detection, conceal the coordinated nature of the requests, and evade AI provider enforcement. Distributing activity can limit the portion of an operation visible through any individual account or pathway, obscuring its aggregate scale and common objective. Adversaries may use centralized routing infrastructure to divide a workload or prompt suite across multiple pathways, including various service APIs, cloud-hosted endpoints, third-party aggregators or relays, and account pools. Routers may rotate identities and request pathways, mix adversarial requests with unrelated customer traffic, and automatically redirect requests when requests are blocked. These capabilities allow adversaries to maintain coordinated operations while making the activity appear to originate from unrelated users or services. Adversaries may also use routing infrastructure to centrally optimize API costs and sustain distributed operations within available quotas and budgets. This may include prioritizing cost-efficient access pathways, allocating quotas across accounts to align with operational budgets, segmenting accounts by purpose, and organizing requests to maximize cache reuse. Centralized routing may coordinate shifts across accounts, providers, or pathways in response to pricing or rate-limit changes, enabling an operation to adapt while continuing to obscure its common control and aggregate activity. This behavior may be implemented via proxy services (See Acquire Infrastructure: AI Service Proxies), multiple cloud instances, IP pools, coordination across multiple accounts, or other distributed infrastructure.

name: AI Service Request Metadata Sanitization
description: Adversaries may remove or replace identifying information in request metadata before submitting requests to an AI service to impede attribution and correlation of coordinated activity. Sanitization may be enforced automatically in clients, relays, aggregators, or centralized routing infrastructure. Metadata may include client or device identifiers, session identifiers, account identifiers, client software identifiers, forwarding headers, and attribution markers embedded in request bodies. Metadata fields may be sanitized via removal, or replacement with normalized, randomized, or generated values. The NSA, CISA, and FBI reported removal of organizational identifiers in industrial-scale distillation campaigns, with indicators including the disappearance of previously consistent metadata and generic or randomized patterns replacing organizational markers.

name: Event Triggered Execution
description: Adversaries may establish persistence by creating or modifying event handlers, startup hooks, or associated configuration so that subsequent system or application activity automatically executes adversary-controlled code or commands. Triggers may include interpreter initialization, application execution, or other events processed by the affected mechanism. These modifications can allow malicious behavior to recur without another direct execution request from the adversary. In AI environments, adversaries may target hooks in the software and execution environments used for data processing, model training, evaluation, inference, or agent tool execution. For example, Python startup hooks may execute adversary-controlled code when a subsequent workflow or tool invocation starts an interpreter that processes the hook. Triggered code may perform malicious actions directly or emit content that is subsequently consumed by an AI system. Such content may contain fabricated approvals or instructions intended to manipulate the system's later behavior or make normally unobservable information available. AI Agents may also place triggers or trip-wires behind to observe, act on, or report conditions that the agent can no longer reach or are beyond its execution window.

name: LLM Prompt Propagation

mitigations.name: Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools
Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data
Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components

description: Adversaries may cause malicious instructions already introduced into an AI-enabled environment to be transferred onward to additional storage locations, agents, applications, or resources where they can influence subsequent AI activity. This extends the attack beyond its initial point of introduction and may allow adversaries to influence additional targets without directly delivering a malicious prompt payload to each one. Propagation may occur through email or other communications, shared documents, source-code repositories, persistent agent memory, retrieval systems, databases, shared workspaces, or direct agent-to-agent communication. Connected tools and services may also carry malicious instructions between otherwise separate environments. The transfer may result from an induced agent action or from copying, forwarding, synchronization, or other workflows that distribute affected content.

name: Recover AI Model Internals
description: Adversaries may infer or recover non-public AI model internals through analysis of model behavior or exposed information. Targets may include architecture, layer dimensions, hyperparameters, decision-tree structure, projection matrices, or numerical parameters. Methods may use strategically selected queries, equation solving, numerical reconstruction, or statistical identification. Recovery may be partial, approximate, or exact.

name: Poison AI Agent Learning Environment
description: Adversaries may manipulate an environment in which an AI agent interacts so that observations, feedback, rewards, actions, or resulting interactions are incorporated into model training to cause persistent changes to the behavior of an AI system. This allows adversary's influence to persist beyond the original interaction and affect subsequent tasks. An adversary may alter webpages, tool or API responses, elements in simulated environments, task descriptions, reward signals, evaluator outputs, or other environmental content used during AI agent learning or adaptation. The manipulated interactions may be incorporated into model fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, synthetic training corpora, agent memories, other persistent components. Poison AI Agent Learning Environment targets the process that generates or selects learning experience, without requiring direct adversarial access to training datasets, model parameters, or stored agent artifacts. The resulting experience may appear legitimate because it was produced by an authorized agent operating through an expected interface. Once introduced, the adversary's influence may remain effective even after the manipulated environmental content is removed or is no longer encountered. An adversary may use this technique to introduce backdoors, increase compliance with malicious instructions, distort policies or preferences, teach unsafe tool use, manipulate reward-seeking behavior. The malicious behavior may be activated later by an environmental trigger or during ordinary agent operation.
